name: Tukang Besi
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 further work by the same author (or citing it for stress) agrees.
catalog_quote: Stress is regularly assigned to the penultimate syllable of the word, and secondary stress is assigned to every second (phonetic) syllable preceding the stressed syllable. [...] The major exception to this is the common case of a non object-suffixed verb followed by a te-marked object, in which case the te is often counted as part of the verb for the purposes of stress assignment

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: The classification 'fixed-strict' penult with alternating secondary stress (stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 01010 (1 = a stressed syllable)) rests on the author's own reference grammar (Donohue 1995 thesis = Donohue 1999 MGL 20), held and quote-verified verbatim at §2.3.2 pp.29-30 (PDF 55-56). No later or instrumental stress study of Tukang Besi was found; the independent JIPA Illustration (Donohue 1994:40), downloaded now, states the same pattern with phonetic correlates. Two refinements both sources mention do not change the class but merit a caution line: (i) the stressless article te is optionally incorporated into the preceding verb's stress domain; (ii) loans with a dropped final syllabic nasal yield a handful of surface-final stresses ([ke'nta] 'potato' vs ['kenta] 'fish'), which Donohue 1995:36 calls a 'fractional' functional load for stress. sources.citation: Donohue, Mark. 1994. Tukang Besi. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 24(1): 39-41 (Illustrations of the IPA). doi:10.1017/S0025100300005004
sources.quote: 'Stress, realised as a generally higher and level pitch on the whole syllable, is almost always on the penultimate syllable of the word. The definition of the word is sometimes extended to include the following (inherently stressless) absolutive article /te/. ... A secondary stress, consisting of a greater amplitude without the higher pitch that is the characteristic of the primary stress, is also found on every second syllable away from the primary stressed syllable.' Then: 'Contrastive stress patterns have arisen from the introduction of loan-words with final nasals; the final nasal is borro
sources.note: Only other primary phonetic description; gives the phonetic correlates (primary = raised level pitch, secondary = amplitude) and the marginal loan-induced stress contrast ['kenta]/[ke'nta] that the record could carry as a caution. downloaded now; confirms penult + alternating secondary.

tone.quote: Stress, realised as a generally higher and level pitch on the whole syllable, is almost always on the penultimate syllable of the word. The definition of the word is sometimes extended to include the following (inherently stressless) absolutive article /te/. [...] A secondary stress, consisting of a greater amplitude without the higher pitch that is the characteristic of the primary stress, is also found on every second syllable away from the primary stressed syllable. Contrastive stress patterns have arisen from the introduction of loan-words with final nasals [...] This has produced at least one case of a lexical difference based solely on stress: ['kenta] 'fish (archaic)' vs [ke'nta] 'potato (loan)'.
tone.summary: No tone: prosody described solely as penultimate word stress cued by high level pitch (Wanci Tukang Besi), secondary stress every second syllable leftward, one loan-induced stress minimal pair.

sources.citation: Donohue, Mark. 2000. Tukang Besi dialectology. In Charles E. Grimes (ed.), Spices from the East: Papers in languages of Eastern Indonesia (Pacific Linguistics 503), 55-72. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics. doi:10.15144/PL-503.55
sources.note: No claim of lexical/contrastive tone anywhere in the chapter; section 3 'Sound correspondences' (p.59, and the 'Stress' column of Figure 3) states that in the Wanci dialect word stress is cued primarily by a consistently high, level pitch on the stressed syllable, whereas in Kaledupa and the southern dialects stress is a pitch change led by sentence intonation plus loudness; section 4 (p.64) adds that Kapota-island speech (Wanci) has a markedly different intonation, often rising on the final syllable. Pitch is described only as the exponent of (penultimate) stress and of intonation.

tone.quote: The realisation of stressed syllables is interesting in the Wanci dialect. Rather than representing a prominence in the word manifested by pitch and loudness, stressed syllables seem to have acquired a consistently high, level pitch as their primary cue, rather than having a pitch change that is led by the intonation pattern of the sentence and co-occurs with increased loudness, as is the case in English and the other dialects.
